title: Analysis tools
practice: Build a short timeline and a small link chart.

lessons.title: Building a timeline
lessons.intro: A timeline puts events from different sources in order. Every entry should cite the item it came from, so anyone can check it.

tryit.prompt: Put these events in time order, earliest first.
items: 18:47 Tuesday: post about a parcel at number 14

sandbox.task: Add three events to the timeline, each citing its item.

options: Cite the evidence it came from
check.hint: Someone must be able to check it.

check.q: A quick way to add an event from a table is…
options: The timeline button on the row
check.hint: Look for the clock icon on rows.

lessons.title: Clock offsets
lessons.intro: Device clocks drift and systems use different time zones. Before you compare times, correct for any known offset. The item's clock note tells you about it.

tryit.prompt: The courier's handheld runs 5 minutes fast. It shows 15:42. What is the true time?
tryit.explain: Fast means ahead, so subtract: 15:42 minus 5 minutes is 15:37.

sandbox.task: Add the delivery to the timeline at its corrected time (15:37 on 3 February).

steps.label: Add the delivery at 15:37 true time, citing EV-005

check.q: A camera clock runs 7 minutes fast and shows 21:07. True time?
Where do you find a known offset?
options: The item's clock note and metadata
Uncorrected times can put events in the wrong order
check.hint: A few minutes can change the story.

lessons.title: Link analysis
lessons.intro: The link chart shows how people, accounts, phones, places and things connect. A link without evidence is only a guess, so it is drawn dashed until you cite something.

tryit.prompt: Match each connection to the evidence that shows it.

sandbox.task: Draw a link between the parcel and an address, citing evidence.

steps.label: Add a link with at least one citation

options: It has no evidence cited yet
See connections and gaps at a glance
check.hint: It is a picture of relationships.

lessons.title: The map and location data
lessons.intro: The map shows where things happened: phone masts, cameras, addresses and points from location data. A phone mast covers an area, so a phone could be anywhere inside its circle.

tryit.prompt: A phone connected through a mast with a 900 metre radius. What can you say?
options: The phone was at the mast
Masts cover an area. The phone was somewhere in range.
The phone was somewhere within the mast's coverage
Right. Cell sites give an area, not a point.
The phone was exactly 900 metres away
The radius is the coverage, not a distance to the phone.

sandbox.task: Open the Statements tab and send the customer's address claim to the map.

steps.label: Send a claim with a place to the map

options: The area the phone could be in

check.hint: Try it on a case with location data.

check.q: A witness's place sent to the map is…
options: A witness account, marked as such

lessons.title: Fact, inference and assumption
lessons.intro: A fact is what the evidence directly shows. An inference follows from evidence. An assumption has no support and must be labelled. When statements differ, compare them fairly: a difference is not a lie.

items: The parcel was probably left at number 14 by mistake.
The driver was careless on purpose.
The doorbell recorded nobody between 13:02 and 17:20.

sandbox.task: In the Statements tab, mark the conflict between the customer and the driver.

steps.label: Link a claim to evidence that supports or contradicts it

check.q: 'The parcel was probably left at number 14.' This is…
check.hint: It follows from evidence but is not stated outright.

options: Note the conflict and look for evidence that resolves it
check.hint: Memory, knowledge and mistakes explain most differences.

check.q: A claim nobody can check is…
check.hint: Unchecked is not the same as wrong.
